svg.text: How simulation timing is modelled

Three layers, strictly separated: token exchange decides *when a target cycle may happen*; timing models decide *what latency the target observes*; the driver decides *how many cycles to ask for*. Wall-clock speed never leaks into target time.
1 — Host decoupling (FAME-1): the target clock is a resource, not a fact
PeekPoke
tokens on demand (step)
FASED
one token per mem beat
Clock bridge
the cycle budget itself
token channels (ready/valid queues)
FAMETop hub + target
Fires one target cycle when EVERY input
channel holds a token and every output
has space. Otherwise the clock enable
stays low: the target is frozen mid-state,
not observing time. ○ = the missing token
that is gating the cycle right now.
Why this is exact
The target cannot advance past a bridge that has not answered, and a bridge
cannot answer early: however slow the host is — PCIe hiccups, a paused driver,
Verilator instead of silicon — the target sees the identical cycle sequence.
Metasim and FPGA runs agree cycle-for-cycle for this reason.
Two clocks, never conflated:
tcycle — target cycles advanced (clockmodule; Vortex PERF: cycles)
hcycle — host cycles spent simulating them
FMR = hcycle/tcycle; target freq = host_freq / FMR
64-core FAME-5 on the V80: 60 MHz / FMR 130–190 ≈ 320–460 kHz of target time
2 — Observed latency: FASED's timing model, in target cycles
The memory the GPU sees is split in two. The functional half reads/writes real HBM through the host memory port. The timing half is a latency-bandwidth
pipe that schedules, in target time, when each response is released. If HBM is slow, target time simply stops until the data is there — the GPU never notices.
target time →
Bandwidth ceiling of this model: 16 outstanding × 64 B / 30 cycles ≈ 34 B per target cycle for the whole GPU — sgemm at 64 cores runs into exactly this.
Counters (totalReads, readMaxReqs, …) are read from the model over MMIO and printed by the driver on every stall report.
3 — The driver's schedule: adaptive step batching (firesim_sim.cpp)
The target only moves when stepped, and each poll costs a thread handoff plus an MMIO round trip. The driver grows the batch ×4 from a floor of 16 target
cycles up to a ceiling (default 100,000; VORTEX_FIRESIM_STEP_BATCH), and drops back to the floor whenever the target goes idle:
Consequences worth knowing:
• “Target Cycles Emulated” is quantized to this schedule — Vortex's own PERF: cycles counter is the cycle authority.
• A short kernel is only *observed* to finish at the next poll; the floor of 16 exists so a launch's busy edge is never stepped over.
• DCR reads poll one cycle at a time (dcr_rsp_valid is a one-cycle pulse), bounded by VORTEX_FIRESIM_DCR_POLL_ROUNDS — slow, but exact.
